Hi, this is the flow we agreed upon last year when we introduced unilateral commission increases-See [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/G01BB0AKNN8/p1669127558910539|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/G01BB0AKNN8/p1669127558910539|smart-link] 

* *For Existing Restaurants*: Transition to the new version of [Special Terms|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/2577203498/Bolt+Food+Terms+Conditions+and+Templates#Partner:-Special-T&Cs] to take effect on the anniversary of expiry of their agreements provided 30 day notice has been given to them of our intention to change to the new version of Special Terms.  Process flow will be:

# *_30 days prior to expiry of Partner Agreement_* send out a notice that we are introducing a unilateral commission and that these will be subject to new versions of the Special Terms. Let the Partner know that if they object to the introduction of a unilateral setting of commissions by Bolt, we will not renew their agreement with us. Restaurants that want to continue with us will be required to sign the new [Special Terms|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/2577203498/Bolt+Food+Terms+Conditions+and+Templates#Partner:-Special-T&Cs].
# On expiry of existing Partner Agreement, sign new [Special Terms|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/2577203498/Bolt+Food+Terms+Conditions+and+Templates#Partner:-Special-T&Cs] with Partners that have no objection.

*So for Partners who are on V5 of the Agreement, send them a 30 day notice of your intention to  terminate existing contract and transition to new contract where according to the Special Terms commissions will be increased unilaterally on 30 day prior notice to them. They have the option to sign new contract or decline to sign.* 
- *If they accept-simply negotiate and sign new Special Terms with them*
*-If they refuse the unilateral commission, then you either  maintain same contract and have to negotiate revised commission rates with them each time OR consider the agreement terminated on expiry of the 30 day notice.*

# No, we do not collect the steps count
# No, there is no additional data collected that can be classified as medical data
# The collected data itself does not contain the Courier identification, only via post processing one can make the linkage. Each timestamp of a movement type transition (e.g. from Walking to Biking) is linked with an OrderID. From the separately collected and stored order data postprocessing can identify the CourierID that was assigned to that order.
# The collected data as part of this data collection does not contain any GPS data nor address data. It is just a list of timestamps and movement type transitions. Each timestamp is linked with the OrderID to know during which order the data was collected. The order data itself contains the delivery address and the GPS traces of the Courier. Postprocessing activity data (combining GPS traces and timestamps) we can identify the latitude/longitude location where switch happened from Walking to Biking.
# With postprocessing it is possible to link the activity tracker data to the CourierID, because we store the OrderID with the activity tracker data. Without the OrderID the data has no value (an unknown person at an unknown place in the world changed from walking to biking at 13:02).
In general we are not interested in the identity of the Courier for our interest, we just want to know where couriers can park and where they walk.

There is a use case called Vehicle Type detection that is interested in the Courier itself. Here the idea is to use activity tracker to check if the Courier uses the vehicle type that they have specified in the app. This is just an idea from the Delivery team at this point. I suggest this is analyzed separately from the data collection itself if this becomes of interest for development.

# As we are not directly storing the CourierID with the activity tracker, we cannot do it directly with current tools. We would need to write and run specific query to connect the data to a Courier and then export it. Doable, but not available currently
# Think about it as a switch. When Courier confirms the order in the Courier app (and grants permission the first time), we send a signal to the Activity Recognition SDK to start sending data to the Courier app. Each time the OS detects a movement type change, it sends us the time and the from/to state. Courier app then sends the data to the Bolt backend server to store it.
Once the order finishes, the Courier app sends a signal to the Activity Recognition SDK to switch off the sending the updates.
# Bolt wants to help Courier partners increasing their earnings by spending less time on deliveries and be able to fulfill more orders per day. One way of doing this is to eliminate wasted time from their delivery. Couriers currently have to make multiple decisions during their trip to restaurants and to customers about where to go, where to park. If we can provide them with more accurate guidance instructions and help them find parking spots, we can save them time. To do this we want to leverage the experience of past deliveries to the same location and learn where Couriers stop when using a car, a motorbike or a bike. Activity recognition from Couriers provides the means to make make Couriers trips more efficient, less frustrating and ultimately to help them earn more.

As in case of the slow GetConnection dbpool issue observed for this (core router) service is the redis slow get caused by the increasing max loop lag, which doubled since beginning of the year (from 300ms to 600ms), meaning the service gets "stuck" for up to 600ms occasionally and responses from async i/o operations like to get db connection or cached value from the redis then sits unprocessed longer over warning limit (300ms in both cases).

if we solve the increasing max loop lag issue then the get db pool connection and get value from redis issues will disappear.

The increasing max loop issue started at the same time as the uncancelable payments. A theory: every cancel reuquest to those uncancelable payments, creates additional related records in the db, then in some part of some flow (not necessarily cancel itself, maybe eg notifications) we fetch all of those records an to iterate over those takes more and more time -> max loop lag go up, increasingly impacting the service.

Translation of second letter:

On 9 January 2024, the police authority sent you a request for information in accordance with the provisions of Section 8(1) of Act No. 141/1961 Coll., the Criminal Procedure Code.

The reference to the above-mentioned statutory provision authorises the police authority to request information that may serve to clarify circumstances suggesting that a crime has been committed. According to this provision, state bodies, legal entities and natural persons are obliged to make requests without undue delay and without payment.This obligation may be refused, with reference to the obligation to maintain the secrecy of classified information protected by a special law or a state-imposed or recognised obligation of confidentiality. Violation of this obligation may be further sanctioned, see as set out below in the instructions also provided to you with the request for information.

In your communication sent on 20/01/2024, you refer to Article 5 of the GDPR that the data provided to a third party pursuant to this Article is thus proportionate, relevant and limited to what is necessary. In this context, I can tell you that the data that are processed in the context of criminal proceedings, so the police authority is bound by confidentiality under the Criminal Procedure Code and at the same time these data are exempted from the GDPR Regulation according to Article 2 of the same Regulation.

It should also be noted that the GDPR regulation to which you refer, so according to Article 4 of the GDPR, for the purposes of this regulation, means that personal data is any information about an identified or identifiable natural person. The police authority is asking for a list of legal persons, so this reference you make to this regulation and the provision of data to a third party, under Article 5 of the GDPR, is completely irrelevant.

With regard to your request to provide further details concerning the investigation and why this information is relevant for the police authority, I can briefly state that the police authority is bound by confidentiality, as already mentioned above, in accordance with the provisions of Article 8a of Act No. 141/1961 Coll., the Code of Criminal Procedure, which states, inter alia, that the law enforcement authorities shall take care not to jeopardise the clarification of facts important for criminal proceedings.

A police authority may only disclose that a particularly serious crime is being investigated under the provisions of section
240(1), (2)(a) and (3)(a) of Act No. 40/2009 Coll., Criminal Code. Justification,
The reasons why the information is requested are described above.

On the basis of the above, in accordance with the provisions of Section 8(1) of Act No 141/1961 Coll., Criminal Procedure Code, I request that you provide:

* A list of all business corporations (legal entities) that are in the Czech Republic in the capacity of a fleet partner for BOLT as of 2020 (inclusive), including the date of commencement and termination of cooperation with the corporation.

Finally, please note that this request and your subsequent response are also subject to confidentiality, according to the Criminal Procedure Code, and for violation, a sanction may be imposed, see instructions.

# fee paid by eaters for delivery - this fee does not change depending on the location of a courier and, therefore is not affected by fraudulent behaviours
## Correct, the delivery fee that eaters pay is calculated separately, before we even look for a courier. Eaters only pay for delivery based on their distance from provider to eater, and the calculations for those are done separately from courier earnings and are affected by, for example, delivery discounts
# fee paid by us to a courier - is this an incentive/bonus paid by Bolt to motivate couriers? Is this a prepayment fee or do we offer this “bonus” from time to time? Is the info about this “bonus“ provided separately to couriers via email/app since it is not mentioned in the T&C?
## Essentially, it is a bonus from Bolt’s side, yes, we call it Marketplace Fee, but couriers are not really aware of it when accepting an order. It’s not offered periodically, but rather calculated automatically upon an order being offered to a courier - [If the delivery fee was higher than the courier fee|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/delivery-order/orders/157349679?cityId=1], then the marketplace fee will be negative, [if it was lower|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/delivery-order/orders/157353430?cityId=1] however, it will be positive. Here are two examples from admin, courier earnings are the first line, and delivery fee and marketplace are the last lines:

!Screenshot 2024-02-06 at 19.30.51.png|width=2283,height=949!


!Screenshot 2024-02-06 at 19.31.12.png|width=2267,height=836!

They can see how much the marketplace fee was in the weekly report, and I believe also in the courier app after finishing an order, but the latter I don’t have access to in order to double-check.
## The elements based on which courier earnings are calculated are communicated to them weekly in the weekly earnings comms and ad-hoc if there are changes. 
## The above means that if we would correct the earnings to what they should have received if the earnings were calculated correctly, we would be essentially doing the same as the Marketplace Fee does automatically. So eaters would not be affected by it at all, and it’s an everyday reality that courier earnings and eater fees are imbalanced.

[Here’s|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1PWTmaOl7eHRg40QtHaVsqm6QJFDregs-ypYdNEVn2Fs/edit] a global playbook on early provider lifecycle, and here’s the [Polish|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1PVitzEGxv4fjdxIHEK-wIEvK58Nkbz_XIZxUVO0YXH8/edit#heading=h.b39xe6d8uduh] playbook. I think they both contain good advice and good practices. I advise that you make a similar action list and disseminate it with the local team.

As a rule of thumb, whenever a new (suspicious) provider is onboarded, it’s a good idea to monitor their performance in the first week and escalate to us if anything is strange. That way we might find some suspicious activity like repetitive cards/addresses etc.

I hope this was helpful, let me know if I can provide any other information.

When TTL is disabled “TTL{{ }}exhausted” is logged instead of throwing a CLIENT_TIMEOUT error, which gives us which endpoints will time out when enabling TTLs.

For example for internal request TTLs: [https://kibana-logs.elasticsearch.boltint.net/app/r/s/FWJkS|https://kibana-logs.elasticsearch.boltint.net/app/r/s/FWJkS]

“Read” endpoints:

* impact of enabling ttl is minimal, since the callers of these endpoints (delivery-basket and delivery-provider-portal) are currently timing out since they have ttl enabled:
* getMenuItemStatus
* {{getVendorProviderAndMenuLinks}}
* getProviderMenus

“write” ednpoints:

* linkProvidersToMenu
* {{updateMenuEntity}}
* {{updateMenuEntityImage}}
* enabling ttl might cause inconsistencies (e.g. for images, we upload the image to image-store but don’t apply image transformation, then we fail to set the item images(
* currently I see 2 alternatives for unblocking enable ttl:
** increase (or remove) the timeouts for these calls on client side: these endpoints are called from delivery-provider-portal where the external endpoints (called by the portal app) have a default ttl of 60s, so in majority of cases this ttl is not exhausted when calling menu endpoints, but then a small timeout (5, 10s) is imposed on the calls; IMHO the timeouts on these calls are way too small, especially since we made them blocking, so it can happen to wait for a few seconds before getting the lock
** use Context.clearTtl to reset the ttl upon entering these calls, which means they will have the default timeout of 8s (or more if set on the endpoint definition in the router)

[~accountid:712020:7a9c1391-243a-422e-806d-72d75be13638], please find our answers for questions 5.3.1 and 5.3.2. below:

*5.3.1 Data Collected, Managed and Marketed*

We only process information that we need, so that we can provide you with the best service on our transportation marketplace. The data categories are as follows:

* *Contact details*: things like name, phone number and e-mail address. For some of our services we might require a little more, like your home address.
* *Profile information*: things like your profile picture, saved addresses, language and communication preferences. For some of our services we might require a little more, like your driver license details.
* *Geolocation*: such as where you need a ride from, or the location of nearby scooters to you, the time, the journey progression and the final destination of your trip.
* *Payment information* like the amount charged and the payment card used.
* *Communication and correspondence records* such as when you engage with our in-app chat, or speak with our customer service agents.
* *Limited identification data of the device*, like the IP address, on which the Bolt app has been installed
* *Data about the usage of the transportation services*: things like data about journey status, times and data about your conduct as assessed by drivers.
* *Data on sensors for rental vehicles*. It contains information such as vehicle speed, engine power, driving style information (including sudden braking or skidding) and the total weight of objects and person(s) on the vehicle and changes in the weight.
* *Other user-generated content* such as photos of parked e-vehicles, feedback submitted

*5.3.2 Compliance with privacy regulations*

Bolt has a dedicated privacy legal team and an independent team of the Data Protection officer (DPO-Team). On an annually bases the DPO-team carries out data protection maturity assessment. A matrix is used with 338 items covering 10 different domains: leadership and oversight, policies and procedures, training and awareness, individuals’ rights, transparency, RoPA and lawful basis, contracts and data sharing, risks and DPIAs, records management and security, and breach response and monitoring. The result of the assessment is sent to the General Counsel for action. In addition, Advice Slips are issued by the DPO Team to the relevant stakeholders with recommendations on actions to be taken to bring the company into compliance with legal and regulatory requirements.

Bolt takes care that the members of the Privacy Legal Team and the DPO-team undergo regular training (attending conferences, IAPP certifications, other training courses). In addition, the DPO team monitors current developments in legislation, case law and the publication of guidelines by the European Data Protection Board (and national supervisory authorities) and passes these information on to relevant parties.

Regarding data protection training for employees: All new joiners - everyone regardless of position - have to do a mandatory training. There are a series of exam questions at the end of the training (data protection basics). The DPO also undertakes awareness raising exercises using  the company's internal messaging and notification system (How to deal with data breaches) and provides additional training. The intranet also contains a collection of easily accessible information pages related to data protection and information security.

I don’t consider it to be a huge risk from the contract law point of view should we issue a single invoice based on the General T&C only, but can’t rule out that customer would be successful in claiming that we should provide per order invoices instead (should it change its mind for some reason).

However afaik it’s more problematic from the tax end - _receiving payments after each ride creates the need to issue an invoice, and some countries can demand the invoice to be issued on the same day while others give some time, let’s say 1 or 2 weeks._ Not sure about LV. Also this might cause friction for Accounting. From the contract law point of view we’d need to provide transparency on this to the customers in the agreement, but even that wouldn’t make it compliant tax wise.

+*Background information*+

25 May 2023 

15 June 2023 (it looks like the Driver signed this on 25 June 2024)

23 November 2023

27 November 2023

I also note in the Whatsaap messages that the driver is informed he was enrolled on a new campaign in September 2023 which contains trip requirements. Hi [~accountid:64269319407493675d48c87e] - thanks for your patience on this one 🙏  

As you’ll know, reclassification risk is probably the greatest risk to our business, which means as a rule of thumb the legal team will always say: _“_{color:#97a0af}*_don’t do the risky thing unless (1) you really_* {color}{color:#97a0af}+*_need_*+{color}{color:#97a0af} *_to, or (2) it’s a confident and well-reasoned decision, and in either case… mitigate risk as much as is practical_*{color}_”_ - if you can confidently navigate yourself into one of those categories taking into account the legal team’s comments (from me and anything else that [~accountid:6149a0e9ba1b34006ab04897] / [~accountid:712020:341b8095-1e4f-44ea-ad93-e6b03a07da4c] / [~accountid:5faa45acf7b30b006e3b121d] want to add), you’ll have scope to proceed 👍

^*^**^*^*^*^*^

+*Background for PY*+ 🇵🇾 

_This ticket is for PY so I’ve focussed on that, but I’ll defer to_ [~accountid:5faa45acf7b30b006e3b121d] _for anything to add on Kenya._ 

Based on the latest info available on our risk management system, GOAT, we currently have likelihood of a ‘reclass event’ (in short, an actual claim or regulator action) currently set at “2/5” (Kenya is the same FYI):

* {color:#97a0af}_5% - 24.9% chance of happening this year; or_{color}
* {color:#97a0af}_The risk event has occurred at least one time in the last 5 years; and/or_{color}
* {color:#97a0af}_The risk event is forecasted to happen at least one time in the next 5 years_{color}

It’s therefore fair to say that PY is a relatively ‘low likelihood of risk’ market, compared with some of our other markets. For comparison, click [[here|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1iRAIxZgCb9EAGtb6nPaPsRG4ExKL-OGSaYcFhz49SNc/edit#gid=0]] to see how we’re allocating our markets into 3 broad buckets of risk -  you’ll see that PY in the ‘lowest risk bucket’. So that’s helpful. But to add further colour: 

# I’m aware that the PY parliament is currently considering legislating further on this issue _and_ that there are unions active - so keep in mind that there is room for rapid escalation. I’ll leave it to [~accountid:6149a0e9ba1b34006ab04897] to add any further comments on this.
# The local team will need to confirm, but it’s highly likely that we are running control initiatives such as acceptance rate blocking and driver score, possibly even online hours requirements. In other words, a model where we will should expect to lose claims _if_ they are made. 

^*^**^*^*^*^*^

Moving onto specifics re: the initiative, I’ll sum up my thoughts in two points:

*(1)* +*General Scope for Market Escalation / Impact of the Initiative*+

There is room for different opinions on what the impact of this initiative and engaging with unions will be and we will never know for sure until we try it out (which itself is a fair justification for trying it out, ideally in a temporally and geographically limited way to mitigate risk - living and learning, etc.). 

Personally, I do see engaging with unions, or quasi-unions (like this), to potentially be a slippery-slope when it comes to reclassification risk. It’s typically employees (rather than independent contractors) that have a right to unionise and therefore engaging on that basis does pretty much concede that there is something more going on than an a ‘raw business-to-business relationship’ (i.e. as we’d ideally like to position Bolt, from a raw risk-mitigation perspective). 

When the ‘quasi-union’ fails to get what it wants (i.e. ‘more’), it may then seek whatever other avenues it has (i.e. claims for withheld earnings). With the creation of this ‘quasi-union’ we may inadvertently empowered a new driver movement / full union. Existing unions may also weaponise the incentive against Bolt, citing the acknowledgment that drivers ought to be represented as indicative of Bolt’s employer-like status. Put another way: I would be making point like this against Bolt in court if I was acting on behalf of claimant drivers.

These are only theoretical and a ‘possible outcomes', but if we are going ahead we must be very mindful (throughout the entire existence of the initiative) of such possibilities and be dynamic to curb any unintended consequences.

It’s worth adding that my comments here are entirely one-sided and are made without regard to _any_ positives of the initiative, so they be considered accordingly. Your own team are the experts on managing positive driver / union engagement and are best able to judge the true value of it 🙏 

*(2)* +*Our engagement with the representative*+

The above is all quite generic but, in the context of this initiative, it’s compounded with the fact Bolt will be paying the representative for these ‘responsibilities’ in compliance with ‘our instructions / requirements’.

Adding this on top of the usual arguments re: Bolt controlling drivers, I’m conscious that the appointed individual may be able to issue a compelling claim that he himself is engaged as Bolt’s employee. 

There are potential ‘domino effects’ from this: his connections could jump on-board the claim train, or it will beg the follow-up question as to why this employee is engaged to represent other drivers (… other employees?). 

The obvious things that we can do to try and de-risk (which apply to all contractors) are:

* which should not command with ‘dos and don’ts’ in respect of their performance of the task, or otherwise take a supervisory function - the more autonomy they have, the better;
* we should not do anything that controls their appearance or otherwise erodes his individuality (i.e. don’t make him a Bolt robot);
* we obviously shouldn’t call him anything, or act in any way, like they are under our control as employees - we are definitely not their ‘boss’. 

On that basis, some thought should to go into whether it’s actually appropriate to limit topics of conversation (as has been mentioned)… it would be better, I think, to give the representative total freedom to make whatever points he wants, with the suggestion that Bolt is unlikely to engage on some topics. This seems preferable to commanding the representative to avoid certain topics, but there is room for different opinions and scope to make a decision either way, if well-reasoned.

Beyond that, it’s not obvious to me how this could be materially de-risked - we would probably have to take this side of it on the chin. However, it would be worth syncing with [~accountid:712020:341b8095-1e4f-44ea-ad93-e6b03a07da4c] (our employment-specific counsel) for his view and input on how this could be best structured. 

^*^**^*^*^*^*^

*→ Summary*: There *_is_* scope to go ahead if there is a high level of confidence of the potential benefits of the scheme, permitting it to be well-reasoned that these potential benefits outweighs the ‘scope for inadvertent negative impacts’. PY is a relatively low risk market, as far as I know, which suggests its a broadly suitable target for trialing an incentive like this. 

It should be noted that our proposed engagement with paying the representative will always carry some risk and it’s unpredictable how much ‘spill over’ there could be in respect of the status of other drivers. We can mitigate this (slightly) by ensuring he has full autonomy and being very mindful to not overstep the mark.

Once launched, if the scheme is not showing its desired impacts, or if the risk in the market is escalating… the plug ought to be pulled. This should be monitored so as not to allow the scheme to linger on longer than necessary.

Another good way of mitigating risks is to limit the ‘risky activity’ geographically and temporarily: you could limit the scheme to a single market, or only to specific cities, to test it - then use that to inform your views on any wider roll outs, keeping an eye on how the risk status of the markets is developing.

^*^**^*^*^*^*^

From a tax perspective, there is no limitation on switching models.  But Business Client needs to be aware of the change in VAT treatments as a result of changing the B4B model.  

* No change of VAT number for Business Client regardless the B4B models.  But different VAT numbers will be used for Bolt Ops EE, I suppose it should have been configured from billing side regarding different B4B models.
* *Intermediate:* monthly invoice will be issued by *Bolt Ops EE (EE VAT ID)* to Business Client (LV VAT ID) under reverse charge VAT (i.e. no VAT will be added to this invoice).  No VAT will be charged on ride fare if the driver is not VAT registered.  
* *Resale:* monthly invoice will be issued by *Bolt Ops EE (LV VAT ID)* to Business Client (LV VAT ID) with local VAT 21% on both ride fees (so more expensive compared to intermediate model) and B4B service fees.  The input VAT on B4B service fees and ride fees would be credible against the Business Client’s output VAT.  

Hope this helps.

256.1€ in the report is not the net amount; it is only the fare breakdown (ride breakdown) which doesn’t take the other components like compensations, cash discounts or campaigns (which you can see in the app breakdown) into account. So, it only displays the ride fare total. 

Net amount in the app, as the name suggests, is the final calculation of their net earnings (all these other components are also deducted/added). 

For the ‘duplicate’ invoices, these are not duplicates. If they open the invoices, they will see that one is the original invoice, second is a credit invoice for this original, and third one is the reissued invoice. That is because the original invoice was accidentally issued in the name of ‘Kanuas Privates’. Then we returned this invoice (credit invoice), and reissued it with correct invoice. Original invoice is from the 31st of October, but we did the reissuing process on the 7th of November.

You can see the invoices here [https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-document/invoices?filter={"limit"%3A25%2C"offset"%3A0%2C"filter"%3A{"created_from"%3A1698664552%2C"created_to"%3A1699528552%2C"is_source_of_truth"%3Atrue%2C"to_agent_id"%3A3991189%2C"to_agent_type"%3A"ride_hailing_driver"}}&tz=Europe%2FTallinn|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/billing-document/invoices?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22created_from%22%3A1698664552%2C%22created_to%22%3A1699528552%2C%22is_source_of_truth%22%3Atrue%2C%22to_agent_id%22%3A3991189%2C%22to_agent_type%22%3A%22ride_hailing_driver%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn]

Hi Audrey,

Thanks for escalating. 

I've reviewed the user's orders and corresponding Beehive tickets. Our system has fraud rules in place to prevent fraudulent refunds from being automatically processed for the eater. However, it's important to understand that while these rules aim to stop automated refunds, they don't completely halt the refund process. Instead, they flag such cases for manual review by the CS team. Ultimately, the final decision regarding refunds lies with the CS team.

At present, details regarding fraud decisions or users' refund history aren't directly accessible in Beehive. However, CS can access information about the fraud decision-making process by navigating to [+User Calculations+|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fraud/userCalculationResults?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22from%22%3A1704707453.132%7D%7D] and selecting "Delivery CS issue" from the dropdown menu for checkpoints. For the specific user you mentioned, our fraud decision for automated refunds was {{reject}}, which is why these tickets were forwarded to the CS queue for manual review. 

Our fraud engine can provide a {{reject}} or {{verify}} decision when it suspects fraudulent refund requests. A {{reject}} decision indicates suspicious refund activity based on the eater's and their related users' refund history, while a {{verify}} decision prompts CS agents to verify/clarify the user's claim based on the issue key (e.g if the user claims that the order was never delivered, the CS agents might need to carefully investigate whether the order was indeed not delivered as the eater may be fraudster and lie). 

Unfortunately, we don't currently have specific guidelines for CS on how to handle these situations, so we rely on their judgment. If you suspect that an eater is abusing refunds, you may choose not to refund them according to the guidelines of your local operations.

If you encounter cases where our decision was {{pass}}, and the eater was able to abuse the automated refund process, please escalate those cases to us. Your feedback is valuable as it helps us refine our rules to prevent abuse. Similarly, if you notice an increase in CS tickets due to unnecessary {{reject}} and {{verify}} signals from the fraud engine, please let us know so we can make adjustments.

I will proceed to close the ticket. If you have any further questions or need additional assistance, please don't hesitate to comment on this ticket.

Cheers,
